marrow__ANAT_CH20_Q001.takeaway: Both collateral and anterior calcarine sulci are described as complete; the unqualified calcarine option makes the printed single-best-answer item ambiguous.
marrow__ANAT_CH20_Q001.displayText: A complete sulcus is deep enough to indent the wall of a ventricle. The source identifies the collateral sulcus as complete, and distinguishes calcarine portions: the posterior part is axial while the anterior part is complete. Because the option says “calcarine sulcus” without specifying a portion, both the keyed collateral sulcus and the anterior calcarine part satisfy the stated property.
emphasis: deep enough to indent the wall of a ventricle

rationales.a: The lateral sulcus is not the source-keyed complete sulcus in this item; collateral sulcus is deep enough to produce the ventricular impression.
rationales.c: Lunate sulcus is not the source-described complete sulcus among the choices.
rationales.d: The source distinguishes posterior calcarine (axial) from anterior calcarine (complete). Since option D names the whole calcarine sulcus without this qualifier, its anterior part is also a valid complete-sulcus example. The printed key B is preserved, but the single-best-answer item is ambiguous.

marrow__ANAT_CH20_Q002.takeaway: The anterior calcarine sulcus is a complete sulcus because it creates the calcar avis; its posterior part is axial.
marrow__ANAT_CH20_Q002.displayText: The anterior part of the calcarine sulcus is considered a complete sulcus because its depth creates an elevation in the medial wall of the occipital horn of the lateral ventricle called the calcar avis. The posterior part of the calcarine sulcus is considered an axial sulcus because its axis lies along the visual cortex.
emphasis: anterior part of the calcarine sulcus

rationales.a: The anterior calcarine part is complete; “limiting sulcus” does not describe the ventricular indentation and calcar avis relation.
rationales.b: Operculated sulci are covered by adjacent cortical lips; the calcarine sulcus is complete here because it produces calcar avis.
rationales.c: The source identifies the posterior part, not the anterior part, as axial.

marrow__ANAT_CH20_Q003.takeaway: Heschl gyrus forms part of primary auditory cortex (Brodmann areas 41 and 42).
marrow__ANAT_CH20_Q003.displayText: Heschl's gyrus is located in the primary auditory cortex, corresponding to Brodmann areas 41 and 42.

rationales.b: Heschl gyrus is on the superior temporal surface in auditory cortex, not medial frontal lobe.
rationales.c: Visual cortex is in the occipital lobe around the calcarine sulcus.
rationales.d: Parietal association cortex processes somatosensory integration rather than primary auditory input.

marrow__ANAT_CH20_Q004.takeaway: The frontal eye field (area 8) lies in posterior middle frontal gyrus.
marrow__ANAT_CH20_Q004.displayText: Area marked D is the frontal eye field (Brodmann area 8), located in the posterior part of the middle frontal gyrus. It controls conjugate movements of the eyes and is connected to the visual part of the occipital cortex. Lesions here cause loss of horizontal conjugate movements. The source also summarizes important cortical functional areas, including Wernicke's area (22), Broca's area (44,45), visual association cortex (18,19), primary visual cortex (17), and sensory association cortex (5,7).

rationales.a: Area A is Wernicke area (22), not Broca area (44,45); Broca area lies in inferior frontal gyrus.
rationales.b: Area B is visual association cortex (18,19) around primary visual cortex, not areas 17,18 as stated.
rationales.c: Area C is sensory association cortex (5,7), not motor association cortex.

marrow__ANAT_CH20_Q005.takeaway: Non-fluent aphasia with preserved comprehension points to Broca area (44,45).
marrow__ANAT_CH20_Q005.displayText: The clinical scenario is suggestive of Broca's aphasia, in which Broca's area is affected. In Broca's aphasia (motor/non-fluent aphasia), Brodmann areas 44 and 45 in the prefrontal and premotor facial regions of the cerebral cortex are affected. Patients have difficulty forming verbal or written words. Comprehension is preserved, but the person cannot repeat or name words normally and lacks fluency. Severe involvement may leave the patient with very few words to express emotions.

rationales.a: Wernicke area is associated with impaired comprehension and fluent but nonsensical speech; Broca aphasia is non-fluent with comprehension relatively preserved.
rationales.c: Heschl gyrus is primary auditory cortex, not the frontal motor-speech area responsible for non-fluent speech.
rationales.d: Striate area is primary visual cortex and does not produce the described expressive aphasia.

marrow__ANAT_CH20_Q006.takeaway: Insular cortex is not entirely agranular: posterior insula is granular, anterior insula agranular.
marrow__ANAT_CH20_Q006.displayText: The marked structure is the insular lobe. The insular cortex is not entirely agranular: its posterior part is granular and its anterior part is agranular. The insula forms the base of the Sylvian cistern, lies between the frontal and temporal lobes, and receives somatosensory, viscerosensory, homeostatic and nociceptive information from the entire body, including inputs from the thalamus.

rationales.b: The insula does form the base of the Sylvian cistern.
rationales.c: The insula lies deep between frontal and temporal lobes.
rationales.d: The insular cortex receives somatosensory and other bodily inputs; the false statement is that it is entirely agranular.

marrow__ANAT_CH20_Q007.takeaway: Fluent but incomprehensible speech with impaired comprehension and repetition localizes to Wernicke area, marked 4.
marrow__ANAT_CH20_Q007.displayText: Comprehension and repetition are impaired while fluency is intact, pointing to Wernicke's aphasia. Wernicke's area is located in the superior temporal gyrus and is marked as 4 in the source diagram. Broca's motor speech area (44,45) is located in the inferior frontal gyrus.

rationales.b: Label 3 points to inferior temporal cortex, not posterior superior temporal Wernicke area.
rationales.c: Label 2 points to posterior occipital cortex, not Wernicke area in posterior superior temporal gyrus.
rationales.d: Label 1 points to frontal cortex, where Broca and frontal association/motor areas lie, not temporal language comprehension cortex.
